period: Worshipped from before 3000 BC to Roman times
summary: Horus was the sky, the falcon, the living king and the healed eye: several gods sharing one name, and you meet most of them today.
look: Look for a falcon or a man with a falcon's head, usually wearing the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt. As a child he appears naked, with a finger to his lips and a side-lock of hair. The Eye of Horus, a human eye with a falcon's cheek markings beneath it, is on amulets and walls everywhere.
story:
Horus began as a sky god, a falcon whose eyes were the sun and the moon. Over time several Horuses came together under one name. Horus the Elder, Haroeris, shares Kom Ombo with Sobek. Horus of Behdet, the winged sun disc, is the lord of Edfu. Horus the Child, Harpocrates, son of Isis, is the baby you will have seen at Philae. And Horus son of Isis is the avenger of his murdered father Osiris. The Greeks matched him with Apollo.

From the earliest dynasties the living king was Horus on earth; the first of his five names was his Horus name, written inside a palace facade with a falcon perched on top. When the king died he became Osiris, and his son became the new Horus.

In the myth, Seth tore out Horus's eye during their long fight. Thoth healed it, and the restored eye, the wedjat, 'the sound one', became the great symbol of protection and wholeness, on amulets, coffins and jewellery. You may hear that the pharmacist's Rx sign comes from it; that is a modern legend.
details: Kom Ombo, northern half: falcon-headed Haroeris, Horus the Elder.
Edfu, over every doorway: Horus of Behdet as the winged sun disc.
Edfu court: the granite falcon in the double crown.
Anywhere: the wedjat eye, with the teardrop and curl beneath it.
fun_fact: The Greeks saw the child Horus with his finger to his lips and decided he was a god of silence, Harpocrates. Egyptians simply meant a little boy sucking his finger.
narration: Horus is the god you meet most today, so here is a quick guide. He began as a falcon in the sky, whose eyes were the sun and the moon. Over time several Horuses gathered under one name. At Kom Ombo he is Horus the Elder, sharing the temple with Sobek. At Edfu he is Horus of Behdet, who flies as the winged sun disc over every doorway. As a child, son of Isis, he sits with a finger to his lips. The Greeks took that for a gesture of silence; Egyptians meant a little boy sucking his finger. The Greeks also matched Horus with Apollo. Every living king was Horus on earth, and when he died he became Osiris, while his son became the new Horus. In the myth, Seth tore out Horus's eye in their fight, and the god Thoth healed it. The healed eye, the wedjat, became the great sign of protection and wholeness. Now find a falcon, or that eye, on the wall in front of you. It will not take long.

period: Roman, hall added under Claudius (41-54 AD), decorated until Decius (249-251 AD); older Ptolemaic temple beneath the town
summary: A Roman-era hall sunk 9 metres below the street: the town grew up around it, and the rest of the temple still lies under the houses.
look: From the souq lane you look down into a pit: the temple floor is about 9 m below the modern street, and you walk down steps. What survives is one hall, the pronaos, about 37 m long, 20 m wide and 15 m high, its roof carried by 18 columns and 6 half-columns in the facade. The cleaned ceiling is overhead. Allow 30-45 minutes.
story:
The temple belonged to the creator god Khnum and the goddess Neith, with Menhit, Nebtu and their son Heka. The main temple was Ptolemaic: Ptolemy III, V, VI and VIII appear in its decoration, and the back wall of this hall is the old temple's facade. Under the emperor Claudius, in the 1st century AD, the great hall was built in front, and decorating it took almost two centuries. The last emperor named is Decius, around 250 AD. These are among the latest long hieroglyphic texts ever carved.

Roman emperors in pharaoh's crowns fill the walls: Claudius, Vespasian, Domitian, Trajan, Hadrian, Commodus, Septimius Severus, Caracalla and Geta. After Caracalla had his brother Geta killed, Geta's name was erased across the empire, yet here it can still be read. When Decius defeated Philip the Arab in 249 AD, Philip's names were chiselled out and replaced with Decius's.

Why is it in a hole? For 2,000 years the town rose on its own mud-brick and rubbish while the temple stayed put. The rest of it lies under the houses. The hall survived partly because it was useful: in the mid-19th century it served as a cotton warehouse. Napoleon's scholars admired it as an ideal example of Egyptian temple architecture.

Look at the capitals: 24 columns and half-columns, and no two capitals alike. The walk down the covered souq to get here is part of the visit.
details: Column capitals: palm, papyrus, lotus and vines, no two alike; compare neighbours.
Walls: Roman emperors as pharaohs, with Greek titles spelled in hieroglyphs inside their cartouches.
Back wall: the facade of the older Ptolemaic temple, its doorway leading to rooms still buried under the town.
Overhead: the cleaned ceiling with vultures, zodiac and stars.
From the top of the steps: the street level 9 m above the floor, the measure of 2,000 years of town.
fun_fact: When Decius beat Philip the Arab in 249 AD, the sculptors here simply cut out Philip's name and carved Decius's in its place. Political editing, Roman style.
narration: You are at the Temple of Khnum at Esna, about 9 metres below the street. The temple did not sink. The town rose around it, layer by layer, for two thousand years. What survives is one great hall, 37 metres long and 15 metres high, with 24 columns. The rest of the temple still lies under the houses behind it. The god here is Khnum, the ram-headed potter who shaped people, together with the goddess Neith. The older temple was built by the Ptolemies, but this hall was added by the Roman emperor Claudius in the first century AD, and decorating it took almost two hundred years. The last emperor named here is Decius, around 250 AD. These are among the very last long hieroglyphic texts ever carved. The walls are full of Roman emperors dressed as pharaohs. When Decius defeated his rival Philip, the masons simply cut out Philip's name and carved Decius in its place. In the nineteenth century the hall served as a cotton warehouse, which helped it survive. Now look at the tops of the columns around you. Palm, papyrus, lotus and vines, combined in different ways. No two are the same. Then look up: the colours on the ceiling are original.

period: Roman, 1st-3rd century AD; cleaned c. 2018-2023, work on walls continuing
summary: For centuries the ceiling was black with soot; an Egyptian-German team cleaned it and found yellow and red skies, a full zodiac and 200 unknown inscriptions.
look: Look straight up. The ceiling is divided into strips between the beams. Over the central aisle flies a row of 46 vultures with spread wings: the goddesses Nekhbet and Wadjet. The other strips carry the sky: zodiac signs, planets, Orion and Sirius, stars, sky goddesses and fabulous creatures. Yellow and red dominate.
story:
For most of its life you could hardly see this ceiling. Dirt and soot from centuries of fires covered it. From about 2018 Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities and the University of Tübingen, led by Hisham El-Leithy and Christian Leitz, cleaned it; about 30 Egyptian specialists under Ahmed Emam did the delicate work. In October 2023 the ceiling was declared complete; walls and columns came next.

Under the black, the original colours returned, and so did writing: almost 200 ink inscriptions, painted but never carved and unknown until now, which name many of the figures. The ceiling is in seven sections, each with its theme: the daily course of the sun, the phases of the moon, the hours of the night, New Year.

The zodiac is a foreign guest. It comes from Babylonian astronomy and reached Egypt only in Ptolemaic times, probably through the Greeks, so this is a Greek-Babylonian idea painted in Egyptian style. Complete temple zodiacs survive only here and at Dendera, where the ceiling is mostly white and light blue. Look for Orion with Sothis, the star Sirius, beside him: Sirius disappears from the night sky for about 70 days a year, and its return at dawn marked New Year and heralded the flood. There are also the planets Jupiter, Saturn and Mars, and odd beasts: a snake with a ram's head, a bird with a crocodile's head, a snake's tail and four wings.

During the cleaning a Greek inscription in red ink, from the reign of Domitian, also turned up on the west wall.
details: Central aisle: the row of 46 vultures with spread wings, Nekhbet and Wadjet.
Side strips: zodiac figures, some of which you will recognise from your own horoscope.
Orion with Sothis, the star Sirius, beside him: the New Year star.
Odd creatures: a ram-headed snake and a crocodile-headed bird with four wings.
Any wall or column still dark: compare it with the ceiling to see what the soot did.
fun_fact: Before the cleaning, many of these figures could not be identified. The painted ink labels, invisible under the soot, turned out to name them: the ceiling came with its own captions.
narration: Look up. For most of the last two thousand years this ceiling was black with dirt and soot. From about 2018, Egyptian conservators working with the University of Tübingen in Germany cleaned it, centimetre by centimetre, and in 2023 the ceiling was finished. What came back are the original colours, mostly yellow and red. Over the central aisle flies a row of 46 vultures with spread wings: the goddesses Nekhbet and Wadjet, protectors of Upper and Lower Egypt. On the other strips is the sky itself: the course of the sun, the phases of the moon, the hours of the night, the planets Jupiter, Saturn and Mars, and a complete zodiac. The zodiac is a foreign guest. It came from Babylon and reached Egypt with the Greeks, so here a Greek and Babylonian idea is painted in Egyptian style. Complete temple zodiacs survive only here and at Dendera. Find Orion, with the star Sirius beside him. Sirius vanishes from the night sky for about 70 days a year, and its return at dawn marked New Year and the coming of the flood. The cleaning also revealed almost 200 painted inscriptions that were never carved, naming many of the figures. Now compare the bright ceiling with any wall or column still dark with soot, waiting its turn.

summary: Here priests wrote hymns to Khnum almost entirely in rams and crocodiles: hieroglyphs at their most playful, shortly before they fell silent.
look: The walls and columns of the hall are covered with dense text. Two hymns to Khnum are written cryptographically, one almost entirely with ram signs and the other with crocodile signs, so they look like the same animal repeated again and again. They are not labelled: ask a guide or a guard to point them out.
story:
By Roman times hieroglyphs had become a priestly art. The script had grown from about 700 signs to thousands, and priests delighted in rare signs, unusual spellings and visual puns. Esna's texts are among the last long hieroglyphic inscriptions, and among the most inventive. The two cryptographic hymns show it best. In each, one animal does almost all the work: the ram, Khnum's own creature, or the crocodile. A sign could carry different sound values depending on its place, so a row of identical animals becomes a sentence of praise, readable only by the initiated. The French Egyptologist Serge Sauneron, who published the Esna inscriptions, worked out how they function.

Other texts are plain and beautiful. A great hymn describes Khnum building a human being on his potter's wheel, part by part: he ties the blood to the bones, stretches the skin over the limbs, makes the hair grow, shapes the skull, opens the eyes, hollows the ears and gives the body breath. He also gave the peoples their different languages. Fourteen columns carry parts of a long temple ritual, and the walls preserve the town's festival calendar.

And who paid for it? Roman emperors shown as pharaohs, Trajan, Hadrian, Septimius Severus, Decius, most of whom never came near the place.
details: Look for a text where the same ram or crocodile sign repeats line after line: that is the cryptographic style.
Ram-headed Khnum receiving offerings from emperors dressed as pharaohs.
Columns: long vertical bands of text, part of the temple ritual that runs over 14 columns.
Cartouches: Roman names and Greek titles spelled out in hieroglyphs.
fun_fact: One hymn here credits Khnum with giving different peoples different languages: an ancient answer to why your Greek and the guard's Arabic sound nothing alike.
narration: The walls and columns around you carry some of the last hieroglyphs ever carved, and some of the most playful. By Roman times the script had grown from about 700 signs to thousands, and priests loved rare signs, odd spellings and visual puns. Two hymns to Khnum here take the game to the limit. One is written almost entirely with pictures of a ram, the other with crocodiles. Each sign could be read with different sounds depending on its place, so a row of identical animals becomes a sentence of praise that only the initiated could read. Other hymns are plain and beautiful. One describes Khnum building a human body on his potter's wheel: he ties the blood to the bones, stretches the skin over the limbs, makes the hair grow, opens the eyes, hollows the ears and gives the body breath. He even gave different peoples their different languages. Now look along the columns for a band of text where the same animal sign repeats again and again. If you find one, you have found the priests' crossword.

period: Worshipped from the 1st Dynasty to Roman times
summary: The ram-headed potter who shaped every child and its life force on his wheel, and kept the Nile's flood in the caves of the cataract.
look: Look for a man with a ram's head. In older images his horns stick out sideways, long and wavy, from an early breed of sheep; later he often has the curled horns of Amun's ram as well. He may be shown seated at a potter's wheel, shaping a small figure.
story:
Khnum is one of the oldest gods, a creator linked with water and with the First Cataract at Aswan. Egyptians believed the flood rose from caverns near there, and Khnum controlled it. His two great riverside temples were on Elephantine Island in Aswan, where his consort was Satet and his daughter Anuket, and here at Esna, where he was paired with Menhit and Nebtu, with Neith and their son Heka worshipped beside them.

His best-known job is potter. He shaped each child, and its ka, its life force, on his wheel and placed them in the mother's womb. On the 21st at Deir el-Bahari you can see him fashioning Hatshepsut and her ka; the same scene for Amenhotep III is at Luxor Temple. Even the builder of the Great Pyramid carried his name: Khufu is short for Khnum-Khufu, 'Khnum protects me'.

On Sehel island near Aswan, the Famine Stela, carved in Ptolemaic times, tells of seven years of drought under King Djoser of the 3rd Dynasty. Khnum appears to the king in a dream and promises to end the famine, and in thanks Djoser grants his temple a tenth of the region's revenue. Most scholars read it as a later priestly claim dressed up as an ancient decree.
details: Here at Esna: ram-headed Khnum receiving offerings from Roman emperors.
Horn shapes: wavy horizontal horns for the old Khnum, curled horns borrowed from Amun's ram.
On the 21st at Deir el-Bahari: Khnum at his wheel shaping Hatshepsut and her ka.
In Aswan: the ruins of his other great temple on Elephantine Island.
fun_fact: Khufu, builder of the Great Pyramid, was really Khnum-Khufu, 'Khnum protects me': the potter god hides inside the most famous name in Egypt.
narration: Meet Khnum, the ram-headed god of this temple. In the oldest images his horns stick out sideways, long and wavy, from an early breed of sheep that later disappeared from Egypt. Khnum was a creator and a water god. Egyptians believed the Nile flood rose from caves near Aswan, and Khnum controlled it, so his other great temple stood on Elephantine Island. His best-known job was potter. He shaped every child on his wheel, together with its ka, its life force, and placed them in the mother's womb. On the 21st, at Hatshepsut's temple, you can see him shaping the queen as a baby. Even the builder of the Great Pyramid carried his name: Khufu is short for Khnum Khufu, Khnum protects me. On an island near Aswan, a stela tells of seven years of famine under King Djoser, until Khnum appeared in a dream and promised to send the flood again. Now look around the walls here for a figure with a ram's head, and check his horns: wavy and sideways, or curled?
